chapter_title: What Is ROS and Why Use It?
chapter_summary:
ROS stands for **Robot Operating System**, but that name is misleading. ROS is not an operating system like Linux, Windows, or macOS. It is a **middleware** — a software layer that sits on top of a real operating system (almost always Ubuntu Linux) and provides the communication infrastructure, libraries, and tools that robot developers need. ROS handles the "plumbing" of robotics so that you can focus on the "brain" — the algorithms, behaviors, and user interfaces that make your robot unique.

Imagine you are building a mobile robot with a camera, a LiDAR sensor, wheel motors, and a joystick controller. Without ROS, you would have to write custom code to connect the camera driver to your object detection algorithm, send the detection results to your navigation algorithm, command the motors based on the navigation output, and display everything on a screen. Each of these connections would require you to design a communication protocol, handle data serialization, manage network sockets, and deal with synchronization. If you wanted to replace the camera with a different model, you would have to rewrite all that connection code.

ROS solves this problem by providing a **standardized communication framework**. In ROS, each piece of functionality is a **node** — an independent program that does one thing. The camera driver is a node. The object detection algorithm is a node. The motor controller is a node. The joystick interface is a node. Nodes communicate with each other through **topics** (for streaming data), **services** (for request-response interactions), and **actions** (for long-running tasks with feedback). Because the communication is standardized, you can replace the camera node with a different camera node without changing any other code, as long as the new node publishes the same type of data on the same topic.

This **modularity** is the most important benefit of ROS. It allows you to:
- **Reuse code:** ROS has a vast ecosystem of open-source packages. Need to navigate a robot? Use the `move_base` package. Need to map an environment? Use `gmapping`. Need to plan a robot arm trajectory? Use `MoveIt`. You do not need to reinvent these algorithms.
- **Test in simulation:** ROS integrates with Gazebo, a 3D physics simulator. You can develop and test your robot's behavior in simulation before deploying it on physical hardware, saving time and preventing damage.
- **Scale up:** As your robot becomes more complex, you simply add more nodes. ROS handles the communication between 2 nodes and 200 nodes with the same architecture.
- **Collaborate:** Because ROS is a standard, teams can work on different parts of a robot independently. The perception team works on the camera and LiDAR nodes. The planning team works on the navigation node. The control team works on the motor node. As long as they agree on the topic names and message types, the pieces fit together.

The core components of ROS are:
- **ROS Master:** A central registry that keeps track of all nodes, topics, services, and parameters. When a node starts, it registers itself with the Master. When a node wants to subscribe to a topic, it asks the Master which node is publishing that topic. The Master is started with the `roscore` command.
- **Nodes:** Independent programs that perform computation. A node might read a sensor, process images, plan paths, or control motors. Nodes are written in Python or C++.
- **Topics:** Named buses over which nodes exchange messages. A topic is a one-way stream of data. Publishers send messages to a topic; subscribers receive messages from a topic. Multiple publishers and subscribers can use the same topic.
- **Messages:** Data structures that define the type of information being sent on a topic. ROS provides standard message types for common data: `geometry_msgs/Twist` for velocity commands, `sensor_msgs/LaserScan` for LiDAR data, `std_msgs/String` for text, and many more. You can also define custom message types.
- **Services:** A synchronous request-response mechanism. A service client sends a request to a service server, which processes the request and sends back a response. Services are used for quick, discrete tasks: "get the current battery level," "toggle the LED," "compute the inverse kinematics."
- **Actions:** An asynchronous mechanism for long-running tasks. An action client sends a goal to an action server, which works on the task and sends periodic feedback. The client can cancel the goal at any time. Actions are used for tasks like "move the robot to position (5, 3)," "grasp the object," or "take off and hover at 10 meters."
- **Parameter Server:** A shared dictionary that stores configuration values. Nodes can read and write parameters at runtime. Parameters are used for settings that should be configurable without recompiling code: robot name, sensor frequency, PID gains, simulation mode.

**When to use ROS:** ROS is ideal for complex robots with multiple sensors, actuators, and algorithms that need to communicate. If you are building a robot with more than one microcontroller, or if you need to integrate existing algorithms (SLAM, navigation, perception), ROS is the right choice. ROS is also the standard for robotics research, so if you want to publish papers or collaborate with other researchers, ROS is essential.

**When NOT to use ROS:** For very simple robots with a single microcontroller and one sensor, ROS may be overkill. If you are building a simple line-following robot with an Arduino, ROS adds unnecessary complexity. Similarly, for real-time-critical systems with hard timing constraints (e.g., motor control loops that must run at 1 kHz), ROS's publish-subscribe latency may be too high, and you may need a dedicated real-time system like FreeRTOS or a custom ROS-agnostic control loop.

**ROS versions:** ROS 1 (Noetic, Melodic, Kinetic) has been the standard for over a decade. ROS 2 (Humble, Foxy, Galactic) is the next-generation version with improved real-time support, security, and distributed computing. This course focuses on ROS 1 because it is the most widely used and has the largest package ecosystem, but the concepts are largely transferable to ROS 2.

screens.title: What Is ROS and Why Use It?
screens.subtitle: Understanding ROS as middleware, its architecture, and practical trade-offs for robot projects.

narration.text: Today we introduce ROS — the Robot Operating System — and why it matters for building real robots. ROS is not a traditional operating system; it is middleware that runs on top of an OS, most commonly Ubuntu Linux. Its job is to solve the plumbing: standardized communication, reusable packages, and tools that let teams connect sensors, algorithms, and actuators without rewriting connection code. Imagine building a mobile robot with a camera, LiDAR, motors, and a joystick. Without ROS you would write custom serializers, sockets, and sync logic for every connection. With ROS each function is a node that publishes and subscribes on named channels, so you can swap a camera driver or update an algorithm without refactoring the whole system. In this lesson you will learn the core components — nodes, topics, messages, services, actions, the parameter server, and the ROS Master — and practical advice on when ROS is appropriate and when a lighter embedded approach is better. By the end, you’ll be able to map robot functions to ROS communication patterns and justify choosing ROS for more complex, multi-component systems.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: ROS is middleware that standardizes communication between independent programs called nodes, letting you build modular, reusable robotic systems without reimplementing low-level plumbing.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: Over the next screens we’ll build four concrete skills that let you reason about robot software architecture. First, you will be able to define ROS precisely and contrast it with a real operating system. That means naming ROS as middleware and explaining why it runs on top of an OS such as Ubuntu Linux rather than replacing it. Second, you will be able to explain the practical problems ROS solves — communication, modularity, reusability, and scalability — and give examples like swapping a camera driver without touching navigation code. Third, you will identify the core ROS components: nodes, topics, messages, services, actions, the parameter server, and the ROS Master, and describe how each one is used in typical robot tasks. Fourth, you will learn to decide when ROS is appropriate versus when a simpler embedded or custom solution is better, for example a single-microcontroller line-follower or a hard real-time 1 kHz motor loop. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the mapping between robot needs and ROS building blocks.

screens.title: ROS as Middleware, Not an Operating System
screens.subtitle: What middleware means and why ROS sits on top of an OS

narration.text: Start with a clear definition. ROS is middleware — a software layer that provides communication infrastructure and developer tools — not a replacement for your operating system. Middleware sits between applications and the OS to make common tasks easier. In robotics, ROS provides the plumbing for message passing, discovery, and shared parameters while relying on a real OS, typically Ubuntu Linux, for process management, device drivers, and hardware access. This separation matters because ROS tools and nodes assume the underlying OS handles low-level concerns such as drivers and real-time scheduling, while ROS handles interoperability and developer workflows. A concrete example: you usually install a camera driver on Linux and run a ROS node that reads from that driver and publishes image messages on a topic. If ROS were an OS, it would have to include kernel-level device support; instead it leverages Linux and focuses on message definitions, discovery, and developer utilities. A common misconception is to treat ROS as if it provides real-time guarantees; it does not inherently enforce hard real-time constraints. If your control loop requires strict 1 kHz timing, you may need a real-time OS or dedicated microcontroller loops. Takeaway: think of ROS as the connective tissue that makes modular robotics development feasible without reimplementing low-level system services.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: ROS = middleware layer that standardizes communication and tools while relying on an underlying OS for hardware and process management.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › ROS as Middleware
What middleware means

Middleware provides shared services and communication so independent programs can interoperate without each one reimplementing low-level networking and discovery.

Concrete example
Imagine a camera driver running on Linux that publishes images. A separate vision node subscribes to those images to detect objects. ROS handles the message format and transport, so you can replace the camera without changing the vision node as long as the topic and message types match.
Why this matters: saves time and prevents duplicated networking code across teams.
Misconception: ROS provides hard real-time guarantees — it typically does not.
Key Takeaway

Treat ROS as the interoperability layer. Use an OS for hardware and scheduling; use ROS for communication and reuse.

Analogy
Think of Linux as the building's electrical system and ROS as the network of labeled power strips and cable paths that let appliances plug in without rewiring the house.
Quick contrast
Operating System: provides drivers, process lifecycle, low-level IO.
ROS Middleware: provides discovery, message exchange, parameter management, and developer tools.

screens.title: Nodes: Building Blocks of a Robot
screens.subtitle: Independent programs that each perform a single responsibility

narration.text: Nodes are the fundamental units of computation in ROS. Each node is an independent program that performs one responsibility: reading a sensor, running perception, planning, or controlling motors. This separation helps teams parallelise work and swap implementations easily. For example, a camera driver node publishes raw images, an object detection node subscribes and publishes object coordinates, and a motor controller node subscribes to velocity commands. Because each node communicates through standard channels, you can replace the object detector without changing the camera or controller, provided the message types remain the same. Nodes are typically written in Python or C++ and run as separate processes that register with the ROS Master at startup. A common misconception is thinking nodes must be small functions; instead, a node should encapsulate a coherent responsibility and lifecycle, such as a sensor interface or a planner. Designing nodes involves grouping related functionality, keeping interfaces stable, and choosing whether to split behavior across multiple nodes to improve reliability and testability. Example scenario: split perception into a driver node and an algorithm node so you can test the algorithm in simulation while replacing the physical camera later.

keyIdea.title: Nodes
keyIdea.text: Independent processes each with a single responsibility; choose boundaries to optimize reuse, testing, and replaceability.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Nodes
Node responsibilities

Each node runs as its own process and performs one well-scoped task, for example reading a sensor, running a planner, or controlling motors. Nodes register with the ROS Master so other nodes can discover them.

Design guidelines
  • Group related functionality so nodes are testable and replaceable.
  • Keep interfaces stable: agree on topic names and message types before integration.
  • Use language fit: Python for quick prototypes, C++ for performance-critical nodes.
Example: camera driver node publishes sensor_msgs/Image; an object detector node subscribes, processes images, and publishes detections.
Architecture sketch
Camera Driver Node
Vision/Detection Node
Motor Controller Node
Common mistake
Overloading a node with unrelated responsibilities reduces testability and makes replacements harder.

screens.title: Topics and Messages: Streaming Data
screens.subtitle: One-way named channels and standard message types

narration.text: Topics provide one-way streams of data between nodes. Publishers send messages to a topic and subscribers receive them. This pattern is ideal for sensor streams and continuous command flows. A topic can have many publishers and many subscribers; for example, a LiDAR node may publish LaserScan messages and both mapping and obstacle-avoidance nodes may subscribe. Messages are typed data structures — ROS includes standard types such as geometry_msgs/Twist for velocity commands, sensor_msgs/LaserScan for LiDAR, and std_msgs/String for text. Using shared message types ensures interoperability: if a new node publishes the same message type on the same topic name, other nodes can use it without changes. Practical example: the camera node publishes image messages at 30 frames per second; the vision node subscribes and processes each frame. Misconception: topics are not for request-response interactions; use services for synchronous queries. Also remember that topics are one-way and do not provide built-in acknowledgment; design higher-level checks if reliability is needed. Takeaway: use topics for continuous, streaming data where one-to-many distribution and decoupling are beneficial. Topics and Messages: Streaming Data means use topics for streaming, typed messages for interoperability, and reserve services for synchronous requests.. In practical terms, one-way named channels and standard message types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Topics & Messages
keyIdea.text: Use topics for streaming, typed messages for interoperability, and reserve services for synchronous requests.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Topics & Messages
How topics work

Publishers push messages to a named topic. Subscribers receive messages from that topic. Topics are best for continuous streams like camera images or LiDAR scans.

Common message types
  • geometry_msgs/Twist for velocity commands
  • sensor_msgs/LaserScan for LiDAR data
  • std_msgs/String for simple text
Example: camera publishes sensor_msgs/Image at 30 Hz → vision node subscribes and publishes detected objects to a detections topic.
Design notes
Topics are decoupled and one-way. Use them when you expect streaming, many consumers, or loose coupling. For queries or short commands, use services or actions instead.
Check your understanding
Question: Should LiDAR data use a topic? Why? Answer: Yes — LiDAR is continuous sensor data and benefits from streaming one-to-many distribution.

screens.title: Services: Request‑Response Interactions
screens.subtitle: Synchronous calls for discrete, quick tasks

narration.text: Services provide a synchronous request-response pattern in ROS. A client sends a request to a server and waits for the reply. Services are ideal for quick, discrete tasks that require a definitive response, such as querying a robot's battery level, toggling an LED, or computing a configuration value. Unlike topics, services are two-way and blocking by design: the client expects an immediate reply. A concrete example: a user interface node requests the current battery level via a battery service; the battery server reads the latest value and responds with a number. A common misconception is using services for frequent streaming data — services are not intended for high-rate or continuous information. If you need progressive feedback while a task runs, consider actions instead. When designing services, keep requests small and responses deterministic to avoid blocking callers for long durations. Takeaway: use services for short, synchronous queries and commands where the client must receive a response before proceeding. Services: Request‑Response Interactions means synchronous request-response calls best suited for quick, discrete queries or commands that need a direct reply.. In practical terms, synchronous calls for discrete, quick tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Services
keyIdea.text: Synchronous request-response calls best suited for quick, discrete queries or commands that need a direct reply.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Services
When to use a service

Use services for synchronous tasks where the client sends a request and expects an immediate response, for example reading a sensor on demand or performing a quick computation.

Concrete scenario
A UI node calls a battery_level service. The battery server replies with current charge as a number. The UI updates its display based on that response.
Misuse warning
Do not use services for continuous streaming or high-rate sensor data; services block while waiting for responses and can create latency.
Design tip
Keep service requests small and predictable to avoid long blocking periods. For longer tasks, design an action instead.
Check
Question: You need to compute inverse kinematics on demand — service or topic? Answer: Service, because the client requests a computation and waits for the result.

screens.title: Actions: Asynchronous Long‑Running Tasks
screens.subtitle: Goals, feedback, and cancelation for extended operations

narration.text: Actions are the pattern ROS uses for long-running tasks that need feedback and the option to cancel. An action client sends a goal to an action server and receives periodic feedback as the server progresses. The client can also cancel the goal. Typical uses are moving to a position, grasping an object, or executing a planned trajectory. For example, a navigation node sends a move-to-goal action to a lower-level controller; the controller streams progress updates and reports success or failure at the end. Actions combine the advantages of services and topics: they operate like requests but provide ongoing status updates. A common misconception is that topics with status messages are equivalent; while you could emulate actions with topics, the action abstraction standardizes goal management, preemption, and result delivery. Design actions for tasks where you need to monitor progress or halt execution safely. Takeaway: use actions for any task that is cancellable or where you need continuous feedback about the operation’s progress. Actions: Asynchronous Long‑Running Tasks means use actions for goals that run over time, provide feedback, and may require cancellation, such as moving to a target.. In practical terms, goals, feedback, and cancelation for extended operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Actions
keyIdea.text: Use actions for goals that run over time, provide feedback, and may require cancellation, such as moving to a target.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Actions
Action lifecycle
  1. Client sends a goal to the action server.
  2. Server accepts and begins processing, sending periodic feedback.
  3. Client can request cancellation mid-way.
  4. Server returns a final result and status on completion or preemption.
Example: navigation sends a move goal; the motor controller provides feedback on distance remaining and can cancel if an obstacle appears.
Why actions?
They formalize long tasks with progress and cancellation, avoiding ad-hoc topic protocols and making behavior predictable across packages.
Design caution
Don’t use an action for tiny immediate tasks; overusing actions adds complexity. Reserve them for truly long-running goals.

screens.title: ROS Master and roscore: Discovery and Registration
screens.subtitle: How nodes find each other and connect

narration.text: The ROS Master is a central registry that tracks nodes, topics, services, and parameters. When a node starts, it registers its name and the topics or services it offers with the Master. When another node wants to subscribe or call a service, it asks the Master which node provides it. The Master itself is launched with the roscore command. This architecture enables dynamic discovery: nodes can appear and disappear at runtime, and the Master helps them find each other without hard-coded addresses. A common misconception is that the Master handles message passing; it does not. The Master only provides naming and lookup services. Actual message transport happens peer-to-peer once nodes discover each other. For distributed systems spanning multiple machines, the Master simplifies connection setup but can be a central point that must be reachable by all participants. Example: when the vision node starts, it tells the Master it will publish detections on /detections; the navigation node queries the Master and subscribes to /detections to receive those messages. Takeaway: the Master orchestrates discovery, not transport. ROS Master and roscore: Discovery and Registration means a registry started with roscore that enables nodes to discover topics, services, and parameters; it does not carry message traffic.. In practical terms, how nodes find each other and connect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ROS Master
keyIdea.text: A registry started with roscore that enables nodes to discover topics, services, and parameters; it does not carry message traffic.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › ROS Master & roscore
Role of the Master

The Master maintains a registry of active nodes, topic publishers and subscribers, services, and parameters. It enables discovery so nodes can connect dynamically without hard-coded addresses.

Important clarification
The Master does not forward messages. After discovery, nodes negotiate direct connections and messages flow peer-to-peer.
Command
Start the Master using the roscore command so nodes can register and discover each other.
Distributed systems
For multi-machine setups ensure the Master is reachable by every host. The Master centralizes discovery but not transport, so network reachability is essential.
Misconception
Don’t assume the Master relays data; it only helps nodes find each other and the topics they use.

narration.text: The parameter server is a shared dictionary where nodes can store and read configuration values at runtime. Use parameters for settings that should be adjustable without recompiling code, such as robot name, sensor frequencies, PID gains, or a flag toggling simulation mode. Parameters are accessible via the Master; nodes query them at startup or read them dynamically if the code checks for updates. A concrete example: set a parameter called robot_namespace so every node reads that value and uses consistent topic names. A common mistake is putting frequently changing state onto the parameter server; parameters are intended for configuration, not fast-changing telemetry. For values requiring high-frequency updates, use topics. Takeaway: the parameter server is convenient for shared configuration and runtime tuning, but not a substitute for streaming or transactional data paths. Parameter Server: Shared Configuration means a shared, runtime-accessible store for configuration values that should be changeable without recompiling nodes.. In practical terms, runtime configuration and shared settings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Parameter Server
keyIdea.text: A shared, runtime-accessible store for configuration values that should be changeable without recompiling nodes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Parameter Server
Purpose

Store configuration and runtime settings that multiple nodes may read or update, without recompiling code.

Good uses
  • Robot name or namespace
  • Sensor sampling frequency
  • PID gains used by control loops
Warning: do not use the parameter server for high-frequency telemetry. For streaming data use topics.
Example
Set a parameter robot_namespace; all nodes read it and construct topic names consistently, making multi-robot deployments predictable.
Pro tip
Use parameter files or launch-time arguments to keep configurations reproducible across runs and environments.

screens.title: Modularity, Reuse, and the ROS Ecosystem
screens.subtitle: How packages and community tools accelerate development

narration.text: One of ROS’s most practical benefits is modularity and the ability to reuse community packages. ROS packages are collections of nodes, message definitions, launch files, and libraries that solve common robotics problems. Rather than reimplementing mapping or navigation, you can use widely adopted packages like gmapping for SLAM, move_base for navigation, and MoveIt for arm motion planning. This reuse shortens development time and reduces bugs because you are building on tested code. Simulation tools like Gazebo integrate with ROS so you can validate algorithms in a virtual world before risking hardware. Collaboration improves because teams agree on topic names and message formats and can work independently on nodes that fit into the same architecture. A common misconception is that using community packages eliminates the need to understand their internals. In reality you must read documentation and test to ensure assumptions match your robot’s sensors and actuators. For best results, treat packages as building blocks: learn their interfaces, adapt parameters, and write glue nodes when necessary. Takeaway: leverage the ecosystem but validate and configure packages to fit your platform. Modularity, Reuse, and the ROS Ecosystem means leverage community packages and simulation tools to avoid reinventing algorithms while validating assumptions for your robot.. In practical terms, how packages and community tools accelerate development. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reuse & Ecosystem
keyIdea.text: Leverage community packages and simulation tools to avoid reinventing algorithms while validating assumptions for your robot.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Modularity & Ecosystem
Package examples
Common packages provide ready-made solutions: gmapping for mapping, move_base for navigation stacks, and MoveIt for arm planning. Use them to jump-start projects and reduce duplicated effort.
Simulation
Gazebo integrates with ROS so you can test perception and navigation in a simulated world, reducing risk and hardware wear during development.
Collaboration
Teams can work independently on nodes as long as they agree on topics and message types, speeding parallel development.
Caveat
Using packages requires understanding assumptions: sensor ranges, coordinate frames, and parameter defaults must match your robot to avoid surprises.
Concrete step
Before integrating a package, run its demos in simulation and inspect topic names, message types, and configuration parameters.

screens.title: When to Use ROS — and When Not To
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs: complexity, real-time needs, and project scale

narration.text: Deciding whether to use ROS starts with project scope and timing requirements. ROS shines for robots that include multiple sensors, actuators, and algorithms that must interoperate — especially when you want to reuse existing packages or collaborate with others. For example, a mobile robot with camera, LiDAR, navigation, and mapping components benefits from ROS’s modularity and package ecosystem. Conversely, for very simple robots with a single microcontroller and one sensor — such as a basic line-following Arduino robot — ROS adds unnecessary complexity. Another important trade-off is real-time control: ROS’s publish-subscribe patterns introduce latency that can be unsuitable for hard real-time loops that must run at 1 kHz. In those cases, implement control loops on a dedicated real-time system or microcontroller and expose higher-level interfaces to ROS for monitoring or planning. Also consider team skills and deployment environment; ROS requires an OS like Ubuntu and some setup overhead. Takeaway: choose ROS when your system benefits from modularity, reuse, simulation, and scalability; choose simpler embedded solutions when tight timing or minimal complexity is the priority. keyIdea.text: Use ROS for multi-component robots and research collaboration; avoid it for single-microcontroller, low-complexity, or strict hard-real-time needs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › When to Use ROS
Use ROS when
  • Your robot has multiple sensors and controllers that must communicate.
  • You want to leverage existing packages for SLAM, navigation, or motion planning.
  • You need simulation and collaborative development workflows.
Avoid ROS when
  • You have a single microcontroller with a single sensor and minimal logic.
  • Hard real-time control with strict sub-millisecond timing is required.
  • The deployment environment cannot support a full OS like Ubuntu.
Concrete example
A line-following Arduino robot: prefer a lightweight embedded loop. A warehouse robot with mapping and multi-sensor fusion: prefer ROS.
Reflection
Ask: does the project need modularity, existing algorithms, or simulation? If yes, ROS is likely the right tool.

screens.title: Simulation with Gazebo and Visualization with RViz
screens.subtitle: Test algorithms safely and inspect sensor data before hardware runs

narration.text: Simulation is a major productivity win in ROS. Gazebo is a 3D physics simulator that integrates with ROS, letting you run sensor and actuator models in a virtual environment. You can develop perception and navigation algorithms against simulated cameras, LiDAR, and robot dynamics before moving to hardware. RViz is ROS’s visualization tool for viewing sensor feeds, TF coordinate frames, and diagnostic topics. Together they let you iterate quickly: run a node that publishes simulated LiDAR, inspect scans in RViz, and test a mapping package like gmapping in Gazebo. This approach prevents hardware damage, saves setup time, and makes debugging easier because you can pause, rewind, and inspect internal messages. A common misconception is thinking simulation always matches hardware exactly; physical sensors and timing differences often require tuning. Use simulation to validate algorithm logic and data flows, then test on hardware and adjust parameters. Takeaway: combine Gazebo and RViz to prototype and validate ROS components safely and rapidly before deployment. keyIdea.text: Use Gazebo for physics-based testing and RViz to visualize sensor data and transforms for safe, fast iteration before hardware deployment.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Gazebo & RViz
Why simulate?

Simulation lets you test perception, planning, and control without risking hardware. Gazebo provides physics and sensor models; RViz visualizes messages, frames, and sensor output for inspection.

Practical workflow
  1. Run Gazebo with a robot model and simulated sensors.
  2. Start your nodes against simulated topics.
  3. Use RViz to inspect sensor data, TF frames, and diagnostics.
  4. Tune parameters and then move to hardware testing.
Example
Run a simulated camera and LiDAR in Gazebo, let the vision node process images, and view detections and scans in RViz to verify topic names and message formats.
Caveat
Simulation simplifies noise and timing; adjust parameters once on hardware for best performance.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let’s summarize the core ideas to retain. First, ROS is middleware, not an OS; it standardizes communication and developer tools while depending on an operating system for hardware and low-level services. Second, nodes are independent programs; design them around single responsibilities to improve reuse and testing. Third, choose communication mechanisms intentionally: topics for streaming data, services for synchronous request-response tasks, and actions for long-running goals that need feedback and cancellation. Fourth, the ROS Master enables discovery but does not relay message traffic; message transport is peer-to-peer. Finally, leverage the ROS ecosystem and simulation tools to accelerate development, but validate assumptions on real hardware and avoid ROS for tiny single-microcontroller systems or hard real-time control loops. Keep these points in mind when designing your robot architecture and picking which components to implement as nodes or offload to dedicated controllers.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to keep in mind

narration.text: These three compact reminders should guide your design decisions. First, name your nodes and topics clearly and agree on message types early; consistent interfaces prevent integration problems. Second, pick the right communication primitive: topics for streams, services for quick queries, actions for cancellable, long-running goals. Third, validate in simulation and then on hardware; Gazebo and RViz speed development, but hardware testing is essential to tune parameters and address real sensor behavior. Keep these rules as a checklist while you design node boundaries and communication channels.
